## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**The keystone describes the vehicle, not the cancellation.** Nothing in the thermal analysis explains why the programme ended, which was a judgement that it had no mission, in [Heppenheimer][ref_heppenheimer_2007]. An article organised around a heat balance will make a political decision look like an engineering one, and it was not.

**The equilibrium glide is an idealisation.** A real entry oscillates in a phugoid about the equilibrium condition rather than tracking it, and the peak rate seen in a real trajectory can exceed the equilibrium value. The treatment here is the standard first approximation. The phugoid about the equilibrium glide is analysed in [Chou 1964][research_chou_1964], [Chou and Laitone 1965][research_chou_laitone_1965], [Woodcock 1966][research_woodcock_1966], [Vinh et al. 1981][research_vinh_chern_1981], [Chen et al. 2011][research_chen_hou_2011], [Pengxin et al. 2015][research_pengxin_feng_2015], [Jie Gu et al. 2016][research_gu_2016], and closed-form and optimal lifting trajectories that depart from it are in [Bell 1965][research_bell_1965], [Chern and Vinh 1978][research_chern_vinh_1978], [Chern and Vinh 1980][research_chern_vinh_1980].

**The crossrange coefficient is taken, not derived.** The relation used is the classical quadratic approximation with a standard coefficient, and its accuracy at lift-to-drag ratios near unity is not established here.

**A cancelled aircraft invites counterfactual writing** and this article tries to avoid it. Whether the X-20 would have worked is not knowable, and the useful question is only whether its reasoning was sound.

## The Source Base

The X-20 has a better documentary record than most aircraft that flew, which is a consequence of six years of a well-funded programme that produced reports instead of flights.

The Dyna-Soar engineering reports are the backbone, covering configuration evolution, structure, leading edges, cockpit displays, pilot factors and aerothermoelasticity. The materials literature of 1960 to 1964 is dense because refractory coatings were the pacing item for every hypersonic programme at once.

The most useful primary collections are the papers Boeing, the Air Force and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration gave to the joint conference of 1960 on lifting manned hypervelocity and reentry vehicles, which include the configuration history, the aerodynamic performance, the Phase Alpha comparison, the hot-gas tests and the Step I flight-test plan, and the programme office's progress report of April 1963. Two later histories from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, Heppenheimer's history of hypersonics and Hallion's history of the Flight Research Center, cover the materials work, the cancellation and the pilots. The Air Force's own history by Geiger, cited in the survey, and the proceedings of the 1962 X-20A symposium are held by the Defense Technical Information Center and were not retrievable from it.

**What is missing is any flight data**, and no amount of documentation substitutes for it.

**The survey rests on 8,022 research records drawn from Crossref, the NASA Technical Reports Server and the Defense Technical Information Center**, of which 1,546, being 19.3 percent, are report primaries by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary. **441 of the 7,853 dated records, being 5.6 percent, were published between 1957 and 1963**, the programme's own years, while 2,671, being 34.0 percent, date from 2015 or later. The median publication year is 2006, and the records fall into 21 clusters.

**The programme's own record is small and old, and its descendants' record is large and new.** The cluster of the X-20 and its programme holds 75 records with a median publication year of 1964, while the hypersonic glide vehicle literature that flies its trajectory holds 286 with a median of 2021.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is read from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is a NASA Technical Reports Server citation or a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. Of the 1,546 report primaries, 1,169 are NASA reports and 377 are Defense Technical Information Center reports.

**The rule reaches the documents this article rests on most**, because the Boeing papers of the 1960 conference and the programme office's progress report of 1963 are held by the reports server, and the Air Force history and the leading-edge development reports by the Defense Technical Information Center. **It does not reach the journal and conference papers in which the engineers of the programme and of its successors published**, so 19.3 percent is a lower bound on how much of the survey is first-hand. The histories on which the narrative rests are books and are cited as such.

### Thin Subjects

**Seven subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the radiation equilibrium temperature of the skin | radiation equilibrium, radiative equilibrium, equilibrium temperature | 4 |
| the stagnation-point heating correlation | Sutton-Graves, Fay-Riddell, Fay and Riddell | 4 |
| thermal expansion of the airframe against its heat shields | thermal expansion | 8 |
| the skid landing gear | skid, skids | 10 |
| the equilibrium glide and its centrifugal relief | equilibrium glide, quasi-equilibrium glide, steady glide | 22 |
| inspection of a reusable thermal protection system | inspection, nondestructive, NDE | 18 |
| terminal energy management of an unpowered vehicle | terminal area energy management, TAEM, energy management | 40 |

**The radiation equilibrium temperature is the clearest case.** It sets the X-20's materials, and 4 titles name it, because the relation is the Stefan-Boltzmann law balanced against the convective heating and lives in textbooks. The quantity it needs is not thin, and the emissivity cluster holds 118 records. The stagnation-point correlation is in the same position, with 4 titles naming the Fay and Riddell or Sutton and Graves forms, because a correlation in use is cited rather than studied.

**The skid landing gear is a subject that ended with its vehicles.** Of the 10 records that name a skid, 9 date from 1970 or earlier, the period of the X-15 and the X-20, and the remaining one is a skid test for the X-38. The equilibrium glide is thin in the opposite way. Of the 22 records that name it, 20 date from 2000 or later, because modern guidance papers use the condition as an assumption and name it only when they analyse it.

**The inspection cost that the reuse argument turns on is a Shuttle literature.** Of the 18 records that name inspection or nondestructive evaluation, 12 concern the Shuttle orbiter, so the cost the X-20's designers did not count is documented mostly from the one vehicle that paid it. Terminal energy management, with 40 records, is narrow but not new, since the earliest of them dates from 1960 and concerns the Dyna-Soar glider itself. Thermal expansion against the heat shields, with 8, is treated in the survey under thermal stress rather than by name.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject**, which is the X-20 and its programme, the boost-glide line it came from and the spaceplanes and glide vehicles that followed it, lifting entry, crossrange and entry guidance, energy management and landing, hypersonic aerodynamics and heating, the hot structure and every other form of thermal protection, the refractory metals and ceramics that carry it, ablation and the ballistic alternative, and the ground testing of all of these. Many of this subject's words also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded. A glide is also made by underwater and oceanographic gliders, sailplanes and animals, ablation is also a medical procedure, a laser process and the surface of an inertial fusion target, and reentry also names the return of prisoners and migrants to society. A ballistic coefficient also belongs to bullets, artillery shells and the orbit determination of satellites and debris, Newtonian also names gravity, modified Newtonian dynamics and Newtonian fluids, and a leading edge is also the leading edge of a cooled gas turbine blade. Emissivity is also the subject of infrared stealth coatings, building radiative cooling, boiler ash and solar absorbers, an arc jet is also an electric thruster and a tool for plasma spraying and diamond deposition, crossrange is also a resolution of radar and sonar images, and an orbiter is also a planetary probe. DynaSOAr is also grid software, Brass Bell a memoir and a philosophical essay, Buran a surname, an opera and an archaeological site, and a skid also the gear of helicopters and the anti-skid brake of aircraft. Missile defence tracking and interception, the orbital decay of debris, air-breathing propulsion, solid rocket motor insulation and nozzles, the microelectronic, nuclear and electrochemical uses of refractory metals and diborides, and the Shuttle's avionics, power and on-orbit environment are excluded as other subjects. Correction and withdrawal notices, abstract and patent digests and one-word titles are excluded as well, because a survey counts research works and those are editorial events or parts of works. Book reviews, reference and definition entries, news items and other notices, and second deposits of a document already in the survey are not admitted either, for the same reason. A signed comment on a paper, a discussion of it and its author's closure or reply are research works, because each argues about a result, and are admitted when their subject is.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Processing and sintering studies of diboride ceramics and of TZM that do not name a use, general supersonic panel flutter, the control literature on generic air-breathing hypersonic vehicles, planetary entry at Mars and the outer planets, and the regulation and economics of reusable launch vehicles each share a material, a method or a vehicle class with this subject, so each is kept and a reader may weigh it accordingly. Trajectory prediction and tracking of hypersonic glide vehicles are kept because each models the glide trajectory itself, and the thermal barrier coating studies cited in the body are kept because their sentence claims only that they are a literature of coatings that keep hot metal below its limits.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** Records read as off topic have been removed, together with other deposits of the same works.

## Epistemic State

**Historical fact.** The programme ran from October 1957, on 10 or 24 October by different accounts, to 10 December 1963 and was cancelled by Robert McNamara without any airframe being completed or flown, with 410 million dollars spent and a further 373 million scheduled. It consolidated HYWARDS, Brass Bell and ROBO as System 464L. The booster moved from Titan I to Titan II in January 1961 and to Titan III for orbital flight in December 1961. Seven pilots were assigned, including Neil Armstrong, and Milton Thompson was the one pilot from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration selected to fly it. The flight plan, the ground tests and the design figures quoted from the programme's documents are historical fact in the sense that the documents state them, and none was tested in flight.

**Published figures taken as given.** Wing area 345 square feet, span 20.8 feet, length 35.34 feet, glider weight 11,387 pounds, empty weight 10,395 pounds, wing loading 33 pounds per square foot, maximum speed 17,500 miles per hour. These come from the reference entry alone, because the inventory by Jenkins, Landis and Miller gives no specifications for the X-20. The programme's own figures, a lateral range of at least 2,000 nautical miles, a 7.5 inch nose radius, a 143 British thermal unit nose heat flux, re-entry and landing weights of 12,000 and 11,700 pounds, and the approach and landing speeds, are taken from the primary documents cited where they appear.

**Source conflicts not resolved.** A gross mass of 22,321 pounds has been quoted for the vehicle, though no source cited here gives it, and it is inconsistent with a wing loading of 33 on 345 square feet. The glider weight of 11,387 pounds reproduces the quoted loading exactly. The programme's 1963 figures give 12,250 pounds for the glider and 5,750 for the transition section, 18,000 together, so 22,321 is neither the glider nor the glider with its transition section, and its basis is not established by the documents cited. The programme cost of 660 million dollars in reference works is likewise not found in them. Heppenheimer and Hargis differ on the temperature at which TZM replaced D-36, at 2,700 and 2,450 degrees respectively. Hallion names Thompson as the one pilot of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration selected to fly the vehicle, while reference works list Armstrong and William Dana of the same agency among the seven chosen in 1960 and leaving in 1962, so Hallion's statement is read here as describing the group at the end of the programme.

**Engineering analysis.** The aspect ratio, the centrifugal relief, the equilibrium glide density and deceleration, the range and crossrange relations, the implied lift-to-drag ratio of 1.350, the comparison of flat-plate impact theory with Lesko's polar, the rescaling of the stagnation heating to the documented nose, the invariance of peak heating with respect to lift-to-drag ratio, the total heat scaling, the ballistic comparison, the radiation equilibrium temperatures, the ablator and heat sink masses, and the landing lift coefficients, energies and friction coefficient are all computed here from published figures and are not quoted from any source.

**Assumed quantities, each of which moves the answers.** A reference nose radius of one foot for the trajectory analysis, against the documented 7.5 inches, to whose square root the peak heating is inversely proportional. A heating constant of the Sutton-Graves form. A trimmed hypersonic lift coefficient of 0.6. An emissivity of 0.85. A lower-surface heating fraction of 0.12 of stagnation. A wetted area of 2.2 times wing area with an area-average heating factor of 0.15. An effective heat of ablation between 3,000 and 15,000 British thermal units per pound. A heat-sink specific heat of 0.22 and temperature rise of 1,000 degrees. Expansion coefficients of 8.0 and 3.0 times ten to the minus six for René 41 and molybdenum and a 1,500 degree rise. Sea-level density for the touchdown lift coefficients. A ballistic coefficient of 50 pounds per square foot and a five degree entry angle for the comparison case.

**A conclusion of the computation.** A thirty-minute heat load does not make ablation impossible. **An ablator is heavy but buildable** at five to twenty-six percent of glider weight, and only the heat sink is impossible. The hot structure was therefore chosen for reuse and was not compelled by mass. The arithmetic permits that reading of programme intent without requiring it.

**Written from present knowledge.** Material postdating the editorial date is used and identified as such.

## Out of Scope

The boost trajectory and Titan III performance in detail. Abort modes, which were a large part of the programme's difficulty. Real-gas and non-equilibrium chemistry in the shock layer, which matters at these speeds and is treated only through a correlation here. Radiative heating from the shock layer as distinct from convective heating. Boundary layer transition, which sets whether the lower surface sees laminar or turbulent heating and therefore moves the surface temperature substantially. The communications blackout. Life support and the pilot's thermal environment. The military missions the vehicle was to perform, and the political history of the cancellation beyond the summary in Programme Origin.

## Conclusion

The X-20 asked what lift costs on the way back from orbit, and the answer this article computes is sharper than the question.

**Lift does not raise the peak heating at all.** Peak rate on an equilibrium glide is fixed by wing loading and is indifferent to lift-to-drag ratio across at least a twelvefold range. What lift buys is crossrange, growing as the square of lift-to-drag ratio, and what it costs is total heat, growing in direct proportion. Two thousand nautical miles of crossrange needs a lift-to-drag ratio of 1.35 by the closed form, which a flat-bottomed delta could deliver. The programme's trajectories needed a design maximum near 2.2 to reach the same distance, so the closed form is a lower bound on the aerodynamics and not a description of them.

**The comparison with a capsule is not the one usually drawn.** A ballistic entry at the same conditions imposes a peak rate twenty-six times higher and a total load about nine tenths of the glider's. The glider's advantage lies entirely in rate, and the lower rate permits a structure that radiates instead of one that burns away.

**The choice of a hot structure was not forced.** Ablation would have worked at five to twenty-six percent of glider weight. It was rejected because it cannot be used twice, so the X-20's most distinctive engineering decision followed from wanting an aeroplane. The heat did not dictate it.

The vehicle never flew, so none of this was tested in flight, although its materials, nose caps, panels and skids were tested on the ground. **What was tested, eventually, was the trajectory, by a larger vehicle with a different structure**, and the crossrange requirement that shaped the X-20 shaped that one too.

The contemporary literature adds a closing observation that is harder on the programme's critics than on its engineers. **Each of the three questions the X-20 asked at once was eventually answered in the affirmative, by different vehicles, decades apart.** The glide went to the Space Shuttle and then to hypersonic glide weapons. The hot structure was rejected in 1971 and is an active research field again. Reuse went to the Shuttle and turned out to cost far more than had been projected.

**The X-37B comes closest to holding all three together**, and it flies the X-20's specification unmanned, forty years late. The cancellation for want of a mission was a fair judgement. It did not anticipate is that the answers would outlive the question.
